learning_objective: 🎯 Open the accounting books! Learn the golden rules of Debit and Credit, how to write Journal entries, and how to post them into the Ledger.

main_concepts.concept_title: ⚖️ The Rules of Debit and Credit
main_concepts.simple_explanation: Every account has two sides: Debit (Left) and Credit (Right). The modern rule: To increase Assets or Expenses, DEBIT them. To increase Liabilities, Capital, or Revenue, CREDIT them.
This is a chronological (date-wise) diary of the business. Every time a transaction happens, it is recorded here first as a 'Journal Entry' with a brief explanation called a 'Narration'.

If the Journal is a mixed diary, the Ledger is a filing cabinet. It has separate folders (Accounts) for Cash, Sales, Rent, etc. Transferring entries from the Journal to the Ledger is called 'Posting'.
Accountants don't just imagine transactions. They need proof! Bills, cash memos, and receipts are source documents. Based on these, a 'Voucher' is prepared to authorize the recording of the entry.

fun_activity.title: 📝 The Golden Rule Story
fun_activity.instructions: Traditional Rules: Real Account (Debit what comes in, Credit what goes out). Personal Account (Debit the receiver, Credit the giver). Nominal Account (Debit all expenses, Credit all incomes). Create a 3-sentence story using these rules for buying a computer with cash!

exam_tips: 📌 Never forget to write the 'Narration' (short description in brackets) below every journal entry. You will lose marks for missing it.
📌 When balancing a Ledger account, the 'Balance c/d' (carried down) is written on the side that is SHORTER, to make both sides equal.
📌 Goods given as charity or lost by fire should be credited to the 'Purchases A/c' because they reduce your stock of purchased goods.
quick_recap: ⭐ The Journal records transactions chronologically, while the Ledger classifies them by account.
⭐ Double Entry System means every transaction affects at least two accounts with equal debits and credits.
⭐ Modern rules group accounts into Assets, Liabilities, Capital, Expenses, and Revenue.
